parts.latex: Which of the following is the correct expression for the indefinite integral of $5^{2x+3}$?

solutions.latex:
From the reference sheet:
$$\int f'(x)a^{f(x)}\,dx=\dfrac{a^{f(x)}}{\ln a}+c$$
For $5^{2x+3}$, $a=5$, $f(x)=2x+3$ and $f'(x)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int 5^{2x+3}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2\times 5^{2x+3}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{5^{2x+3}}{2\ln 5}+c\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int \left(e^{2x} + e^{2x+1}\right) dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x} + \dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x+1} + c \\ &= \dfrac{e^{2x} + e^{2x+1}}{2} + c \\ &= \dfrac{e^{2x}(1+e)}{2} + c \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: What is the primitive function of $8x\times 4^{x^2+6}$?

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2+6)=2x$, write $8x=4\times2x$ and use
$$\int f'(x)\,a^{f(x)}\,dx=\dfrac{a^{f(x)}}{\ln a}+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int 8x\times4^{x^2+6}\,dx&=4\int 2x\times4^{x^2+6}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{4\times4^{x^2+6}}{\ln4}+c\\&=\dfrac{4^{x^2+7}}{\ln4}+c\end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=e^{3x} & v&=1+3x\\u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(1+3x)\right]&=3e^{3x}+3e^{3x}(1+3x)\\ &=3e^{3x}\big(1+(1+3x)\big)\\ &=3e^{3x}(2+3x)\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $3e^{3x}(2+3x)$ is the derivative of $e^{3x}(1+3x)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int(2+3x)e^{3x}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int 3e^{3x}(2+3x)\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}(1+3x)+C\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^{1}e^{3x}\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}\right]_{-1}^{1} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^3-\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-3} \\ &= \dfrac{e^3}{3}-\dfrac{1}{3e^3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Which of the following is the integral of

$$\int(e^x+2)^2\,dx\,?$$

solutions.latex:
Expand the square, then integrate term by term.
$$\begin{aligned}\int(e^x+2)^2\,dx&=\int\big(e^{2x}+4e^x+4\big)\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}+4e^x+4x+c\end{aligned}$$

Integrate term by term:
$$\begin{aligned}\int\left(e^{-x}-\dfrac{4}{2x+1}\right)dx&=-e^{-x}-2\ln|2x+1|+c\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substantially correct solution, or equivalent merit

1945.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=a^x$, where $a>1$. Also shown on the diagram are 4 inner rectangles of width 1 unit.

\exfigure{402_q21_1}

figures.cap: graph of y=a^x with 4 inner rectangles of width 1 on x from 0 to 4, NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Show that the area of the 4 rectangles is $\dfrac{a^4-1}{a-1}\ u^2$.
By finding the area under the curve $y=a^x$ between $x=0$ and $x=4$, and using the result in part (i), prove that $\ln a<a-1$.

solutions.latex:
Each rectangle has width $1$, and its height is the value of the curve at the left end of its strip: $a^0,\ a^1,\ a^2,\ a^3$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=1.1+1\cdot a+1\cdot a^2+1\cdot a^3\\ &=1+a+a^2+a^3\end{aligned}$$
This is a geometric series with first term $1$, common ratio $a$ and $4$ terms, so $S_n=\dfrac{T_1\left(r^n-1\right)}{r-1}$ gives
$$A=\dfrac{1\cdot\left(a^4-1\right)}{a-1}=\dfrac{a^4-1}{a-1}\text{ u}^2$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 2 marks for the full solution (show how to get the area of each rectangle and state the G.P. with $r=a$, $a=1$)

solutions.latex:
The area under the curve:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4a^x\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}\right]_0^4\\ &=\dfrac{a^4-1}{\ln a}\end{aligned}$$
The curve is increasing, so the inner rectangles lie under it and their area is less than the area under the curve:
$$\dfrac{a^4-1}{a-1}<\dfrac{a^4-1}{\ln a}$$
Since $a>1$, the quantities $a^4-1$, $a-1$ and $\ln a$ are all positive. Divide both sides by $a^4-1$, then take reciprocals of the positive sides, which reverses the inequality:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{a-1}&<\dfrac{1}{\ln a}\\ a-1&>\ln a\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \ln a<a-1$$

parts.latex: Give the simplest exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^1 3^x\,dx$.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 3^x\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{3^x}{\ln3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{\ln3}-\dfrac{1}{\ln3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\ln3} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\displaystyle\int a^x\,dx=\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$ with $a=\dfrac{1}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right)^{x}dx&=\dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^x}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}+C \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{5^x}}{\ln 1-\ln 5}+C \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{5^x}}{-\ln 5}+C \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{5^x}\times\dfrac{1}{\ln 5}+C \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 5\cdot 5^x}+C \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.
